# The server was part of the appliance.

A vendor has announced that it will close the cloud service behind its connected home devices. The advertised explanation may be orderly: the company is ending support for an aging product line and giving customers time to prepare. But the practical problem is less tidy. The server was sold as though it were merely backstage infrastructure—when it disappears, part of the appliance disappears with it.

Which parts fail depends on where the vendor put the intelligence. Any feature that must contact the service (cloud-dependent automation) will stop when that service shuts down. Remote access may vanish because the app can't find the vendor gateway. Scheduled routines may fail if their timers live on company systems. Account-based controls (authentication and household sharing) may become unavailable even on a working local network. The plastic, motors, sensors, and radios remain—but the product doesn't necessarily remain functional.

The same problem reaches integrations. A switch may still switch when pressed, while voice commands (requests routed through an outside platform) stop working. A camera may continue sensing motion but lose notifications, remote viewing, or cloud recordings. A thermostat may still accept a temperature at the wall while its app, history, and automations go dark. These aren't decorative extras if the vendor promoted them as ordinary uses of the appliance.

What, then, did the customer buy? The original transaction looked like a durable-goods sale, not a short lease on software that happened to include hardware. The buyer paid once for a device whose important controls were presented through an app (a phone app supplied with the product). If the vendor can later remove those controls by switching off a server, the bargain changes after the money and hardware have changed hands.

A shutdown may be lawful under the terms attached to an account, and maintaining old infrastructure may carry real costs. Security also matters: abandoned servers can become liabilities, and a company shouldn't promise endless operation of an unsafe system. Those concessions narrow the dispute; they do not resolve it. A contract describing broad termination rights is not the same thing as a product designed to survive termination.

Local operation would protect the device from that single point of failure. Core controls should execute inside the home (during an internet outage, for example), with schedules and automations stored on the appliance or a local controller. Essential configuration shouldn't require a live vendor account. If cloud access ends, the local interface could keep the hardware useful—more like losing a concierge than losing the front door.

Local operation also protects privacy and competition. Commands processed in the home needn't become a continuing record on company systems. A documented local interface (the code other software uses to communicate) could let another app or controller replace the discontinued service. That doesn't require every product to expose every security-sensitive function. It requires a supported path for basic operation that does not depend forever on one company.

Manufacturers could go further by offering an export tool for settings, automation rules, and recordings; publishing a local protocol; or transferring service to a capable operator. An optional local hub (a small controller inside the home) could preserve features that individual devices lack the power to run. None of these measures guarantees eternal compatibility. They do make an orderly shutdown possible without turning purchased equipment into a box of stranded parts.

Cloud features can add convenience, updates, and computing power that small appliances won't provide alone. The objection isn't that a product ever contacts a server. It is that the seller may make the server indispensable while presenting the hardware as something the customer owns. Cloud service should extend a connected appliance, not secretly constitute it.

We believe the public-interest standard is straightforward: when a company sells durable hardware, its essential functions should survive the end of the seller's service (with safe local credentials and clear reset procedures). Our demand to manufacturers is equally concrete—design for local control, disclose every cloud dependency before purchase, and publish a shutdown plan while the engineers who understand the system are still there. If your device depends on a distant server, ask the vendor now what will work when that server is gone.
